head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Rearranges the list in place into a min-heap (priority queue whose smallest item is at index 0) in O(n)
Removes and returns the smallest item, O(log n)
Inserts the negated value, keeping the heap property, O(log n)
Total of the heap's items (order inside the heap does not matter)

p: `[4,2,3]`, `k = 1`: negate the smallest once.

blocks.h: Why negate the smallest each time?
p: Negating the smallest value changes the sum the most in our favour: a negative number becomes positive (gain 2·|x|). When all numbers are non-negative, the smallest has the smallest loss. A value negated twice returns to itself, so extra turns on a zero or on the same element are harmless pairs.
Spare turns example: `[-4,-2,-3]` with `k = 4`: each pop shows the smallest value now at the front.

bullets: Space: O(1) extra; it modifies the input list in place.

1005.takeaway: Greedy with a min-heap: flip the current smallest element k times.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Index of the next unused preorder value, shared by all recursive calls (nonlocal)
A single moving cursor over a sequence
Builds the subtree whose values must all be ≤ bound
The next value belongs to an ancestor's right side, so this subtree is empty
Left subtree: values below the root. Right subtree: values above the root but still within the old bound

p: `[8,5,1,7,10,12]`. Each created node and the bound that applied when it was created:

Values arrive in preorder, so a value smaller than the current root goes left, and a larger one cannot belong inside the left subtree. Passing only the upper bound is enough: any value ≤ bound is accepted by the current call; values bigger than the bound must be placed by an ancestor. The lower bound is implied because the cursor only moves forward.

bullets: Time: O(n): each value is placed once and the cursor never goes backward.
Space: O(h) recursion, h = tree height.

1008.takeaway: Build a BST (Binary Search Tree) from preorder in O(n): a shared cursor plus an upper bound for each recursive call.

blocks.h: Why can we binary search on capacity?
p: Feasibility is monotone: a larger capacity never needs more days. So the capacities split into 'too small' then 'enough', and binary search finds the boundary. The check itself is greedy: filling each day as full as possible never hurts.

1011.takeaway: Binary search on the answer (capacity) with a greedy day-counting check.

blocks.h: Why check the direction after one pass?
p: If the robot ends facing north and away from the origin, every repetition moves it farther in the same direction: unbounded. If it faces any other direction, repeating the instructions at most four times rotates the displacement back to a loop. So one pass is enough to decide.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: while i >= 0 and arr[i] <= arr[i + 1]: i -= 1
Scans from the right for the first position where the order drops (arr[i] > arr[i+1]); everything to its right is non-decreasing
Array is already non-decreasing, i.e. the smallest permutation
From the right, finds the largest value smaller than arr[i]
With duplicates, uses the leftmost copy so the result is the largest possible; the swap puts the larger value at a more significant position

head: step
rows: first i from the right with arr[i] > arr[i+1]: i = 1 (value 9)
largest value smaller than 9 on the right: j = 4 (value 7)

bullets: Then `[3,1,1,3]` gives: first i from the right with arr[i] > arr[i+1]: i = 0 (value 3); largest value smaller than 3 on the right: j = 2 (value 1); leftmost among equal values: j = 1; swap → [1, 3, 1, 3].

p: For `[3,1,1,3]` swapping the 3 at the front with the first 1 gives `[1,3,1,3]`, while swapping with the second 1 gives `[1,1,3,3]`, which is smaller. The goal is the LARGEST smaller permutation, so the code picks the first (leftmost) of the equal values, giving `[1,3,1,3]`.

1053.takeaway: Previous permutation with one swap: find the rightmost drop, swap with the largest smaller value to its right (leftmost copy).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: If the two strings are built from a common repeating block, concatenation commutes; otherwise no common divisor string exists
Greatest common divisor of the lengths (from `math`): the longest possible block length
The block is a prefix of the string

p: `"ABCABCABC"` and `"ABCABC"`:
bullets: A failing case: `"LEET"` and `"CODE"` give different concatenations (`LEETCODE` vs `CODELEET`), so the answer is the empty string.

blocks.h: Why does the concatenation test work?
p: If both strings are repetitions of a block X, then str1 + str2 and str2 + str1 are both repetitions of X, so they are equal. If they are equal, the two strings commute and share a common period (a known property of words). The block length must divide both lengths, and the largest choice is their gcd.

bullets: Time: O(n + m) for the concatenations and comparison.

1071.takeaway: Strings share a divisor iff s1+s2 == s2+s1; the answer is the prefix whose length is gcd of the two lengths.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: for top … for bottom in range(top, m)
Fixes a band of rows from `top` to `bottom`
Column sums of the band, updated incrementally as the band grows by one row
Counts of prefix sums seen so far in this band; the empty prefix has sum 0 once
Subarray sum equals target (prefix sums + hash map)
Number of earlier prefixes that make a subarray with sum target ending here; a Counter returns 0 for missing keys

blocks.h: Why does a 2-D problem reduce to the 1-D subarray problem?
p: Any submatrix is a band of rows (top to bottom) and a range of columns. Summing the band's rows column-wise turns it into an array, and a range of columns is then a subarray of that array. 'Number of subarrays with sum = target' is solved in linear time with prefix sums and a hash map.

1074.takeaway: Fix a row band, collapse it to column sums, and count target-sum subarrays with a prefix-sum counter.

blocks.h: Why count groups instead of checking connectivity each time?

p: Skills `java=bit0, nodejs=bit1, reactjs=bit2`. After each person, the best team found for each reachable skill set (binary masks):
bullets: Full mask `111` is reached by team `[0, 2]`.

blocks.h: Why a dict keyed by mask?
p: There are up to 2^16 skill subsets, but only a few are reachable. A dict stores just those, and each person updates the states that exist at that moment. Because the loop uses `list(dp.items())`, a person is added at most once per state in a round.

bullets: Time: O(P · reachable states) ≤ O(P · 2^S), P people and S skills.

1125.takeaway: Bitmask DP in a dict: for each person, extend every reachable skill set and keep the smallest team per set.

blocks.h: Why the diagonal on a match and `max` otherwise?
p: If the last characters match, using them together is never worse than skipping either. If they differ, at least one of them is not in the common subsequence, so the answer is the better of dropping one.

bullets: Space: O(m·n); a rolling pair of rows reduces it to O(min(m, n)).
